questions.q: On what does the editorial say a community’s development depends?
options: Keeping apart from the mainstream
Not quite. The article says: Its own struggle and merit in open competition, not favours from government.
Special institutions set up on its behalf
Not quite. The article says: Its own struggle and merit in open competition, not favours from government.
The goodwill of political leaders
Not quite. The article says: Its own struggle and merit in open competition, not favours from government.
Its own struggle and merit in open competition, not favours from government
Yes. Favours weaken incentive.
questions.rationale: “Development is a goal that can be achieved only through self-struggle… Progress can be attained only in an environment of competition and challenge, and not through favours granted.”

questions.article: The Miracle of Not Getting Agitated
questions.q: A Mongol prince told Shaykh Jamal al-Din that a dog was worth more than a Persian. How did the Shaykh reply?
options: By pleading for his life
Not quite. The article says: Calmly: “Yes, if we had not the true faith, we should indeed be worse than the dogs”.
By refusing to speak
Not quite. The article says: Calmly: “Yes, if we had not the true faith, we should indeed be worse than the dogs”.
With an insult of his own
Not quite. The article says: Calmly: “Yes, if we had not the true faith, we should indeed be worse than the dogs”.
Calmly: “Yes, if we had not the true faith, we should indeed be worse than the dogs”
Right. The answer stirred the prince’s interest instead of his anger.
questions.rationale: “Had Shaykh Jamal al-Din responded… by getting provoked and angry, it would have given a completely different turn to history.”

questions.article: The Miracle of Not Getting Agitated
questions.q: Why, according to the article, does a calm reply to harsh words work so well?
options: A calm reply confuses the other person
Not quite. The article says: Anger provokes the other person’s ego, while a balanced answer awakens his conscience.
Anger provokes the other person’s ego, while a balanced answer awakens his conscience
Yes. Every person is a friend, actual or potential.
Harsh words are soon forgotten
Not quite. The article says: Anger provokes the other person’s ego, while a balanced answer awakens his conscience.
People respect those who show no feeling
Not quite. The article says: Anger provokes the other person’s ego, while a balanced answer awakens his conscience.
questions.rationale: “If you react by getting angry, it will provoke the ego of the person you are reacting to… if you reply in a balanced manner, it awakens the other person’s conscience.”

questions.q: What does the article say listening patiently to a view you disagree with does for you?
options: It obliges you to agree
Not quite. The article says: It enriches your own thinking and keeps the mind fresh, like a flowing river.
It wastes time better spent speaking
Not quite. The article says: It enriches your own thinking and keeps the mind fresh, like a flowing river.
It enriches your own thinking and keeps the mind fresh, like a flowing river
Well read. Listening is not the same as accepting.
It weakens your convictions
Not quite. The article says: It enriches your own thinking and keeps the mind fresh, like a flowing river.
questions.rationale: “Lending a patient audience to a dissenting opinion is equivalent to enriching one’s own thought process… His mind becomes like a flowing river which never gets stagnant.”

questions.q: Visiting a sick man, the Prophet said, “God willing, it will be a means of purification.” How does the article explain this?
options: Illness makes a believer feel his helplessness and turns him towards God, with kindness and humility
Correct. Bodily illness can serve spiritual health.
Illness excuses a person from all duties
Not quite. The article says: Illness makes a believer feel his helplessness and turns him towards God, with kindness and humility.
Sins are removed by a hidden process, whatever the person does
Not quite. The article says: Illness makes a believer feel his helplessness and turns him towards God, with kindness and humility.
Only the sick can be forgiven
Not quite. The article says: Illness makes a believer feel his helplessness and turns him towards God, with kindness and humility.
questions.rationale: “When a believer falls sick, he discovers his helplessness… Sickness becomes a means for him to come near to God.”

questions.q: George Bernard Shaw, who opposed smoking, wrote an angry line that ended up selling more cigarettes. What lesson does the article draw?
options: If your words will produce the opposite of what you intend, it is wiser to stay silent
Yes. An action is right when its result is right.
Advertising cannot be trusted
Not quite. The article says: If your words will produce the opposite of what you intend, it is wiser to stay silent.
Famous people should never give opinions
Not quite. The article says: If your words will produce the opposite of what you intend, it is wiser to stay silent.
Anger makes a person persuasive
Not quite. The article says: If your words will produce the opposite of what you intend, it is wiser to stay silent.
questions.rationale: “If the result of what you say will turn out to be just the opposite of what you intend, it is better that you stay quiet.”

questions.q: What does the article say the Quran’s repeated address “O mankind” implies about the world?
options: That it is divided into friendly and hostile lands
Not quite. The article says: That it is the home of all human beings, to be treated as one family.
That it is the home of all human beings, to be treated as one family
Right. Dividing it into “ours” and “theirs” breeds separatism.
That it belongs to one community
Not quite. The article says: That it is the home of all human beings, to be treated as one family.
That it is of no importance
Not quite. The article says: That it is the home of all human beings, to be treated as one family.
questions.rationale: “According to this, the whole world is ‘Dar al-Insan’ or the land of human beings… Islam believes in the human family concept.”

questions.q: What are the “unilateral ethics” the article asks of a believer?
options: To be good only to those who are good to him
Not quite. The article says: To go on wishing others well and not complain or react, however they behave.
To demand an apology before forgiving
Not quite. The article says: To go on wishing others well and not complain or react, however they behave.
To keep a record of wrongs done to him
Not quite. The article says: To go on wishing others well and not complain or react, however they behave.
To go on wishing others well and not complain or react, however they behave
Yes. He looks to God alone for reward.
questions.rationale: “A believer must adopt unilateral ethics. That is, he must not complain about the actions of others… No matter how others might behave, the believer relates every experience to God.”

questions.q: How did Joseph treat the brothers who had thrown him into a well, when they later came to Egypt?
options: He forgave them and welcomed them warmly
Exactly. He bore no hatred or wish for revenge.
He had them imprisoned
Not quite. The article says: He forgave them and welcomed them warmly.
He refused to see them
Not quite. The article says: He forgave them and welcomed them warmly.
He sent them away without grain
Not quite. The article says: He forgave them and welcomed them warmly.
questions.rationale: “Joseph did not harbour any hatred or feelings of revenge towards them. Instead, he forgave them and gave them a warm welcome in Egypt.”

questions.q: In place of “success versus failure,” what way of seeing life’s outcomes does the article propose?
options: “Success versus experience” – a defeat is experience that prepares for a second chance
Well reasoned. Lincoln lost many times before he won.
“Winning versus quitting”
Not quite. The article says: “Success versus experience” – a defeat is experience that prepares for a second chance.
“Success versus luck”
Not quite. The article says: “Success versus experience” – a defeat is experience that prepares for a second chance.
“Effort versus reward”
Not quite. The article says: “Success versus experience” – a defeat is experience that prepares for a second chance.
questions.rationale: “You should not take defeat as something final. You should take defeat as experience.”
